pages.title: Word frequency and picture-naming time
pages.c: Oldfield and Wingfield asked people to name pictures of objects and related their response times to the frequency of the object names. More frequent names were produced faster. The relation was approximately linear when frequency was expressed on a logarithmic scale. This makes frequency a useful predictor of naming time, but it also raises a design problem because **frequent words tend to be shorter**.
support: If the high-frequency names are also short, the experiment changes frequency and length together. Either property could contribute to a difference in naming time. A confound is a variable that covaries with the intended manipulation and supplies another explanation for the observed result.
pages.d: The dependent variable is how long naming takes. Frequency is the property of interest, while length is a competing explanation that must be addressed in the materials. Finding a clear relationship on a graph is only the beginning of identifying which property accounts for it.
pages.visual: The horizontal axis gives log frequency of occurrence, and the vertical axis gives response latency in milliseconds. The downward trend means that higher-frequency names have shorter naming latencies. The object drawings illustrate the picture-naming task rather than being an additional manipulation.

pages.title: Using a lexical database to examine word properties
pages.c: A lexical database brings information about many words together in a form that can be searched and compared. The English Lexicon Project provides lexical characteristics and behavioral information from naming and lexical-decision tasks. This allows researchers to examine properties of candidate stimuli instead of relying only on their intuitions about which words are common or similar.
support: A stimulus-selection question can be answered at the level of word properties or behavioral responses. For example, a researcher can obtain a list with specified lexical characteristics, or inspect naming and lexical-decision data. These resources make correlations among word properties visible before the materials are selected.
pages.d: The methodological purpose is to connect the intended manipulation to actual measurements of the words. A list described informally as frequent may also differ in length or another characteristic. Database information provides a way to identify and address those relationships during stimulus design.
pages.visual: The homepage offers separate links for generating word and nonword lists and for accessing trial-level lexical-decision and naming data. Those links distinguish selecting stimulus properties from examining participants’ responses to stimuli.

pages.title: Querying word properties
pages.c: The word-query tools support two complementary ways of obtaining lexical information. A researcher can generate a new list of items that meet specified characteristics, or submit an existing list and retrieve the characteristics of those words. The choice depends on whether the researcher is building a stimulus set or checking a set already under consideration.
support: Generating a list is useful when a study requires particular ranges of frequency or length. Looking up an existing list is useful when the candidate words have already been chosen for another reason, such as belonging to a semantic category. In both cases, the measurements can reveal unintended differences between conditions.
pages.d: Stimulus design often alternates between searching and checking. A desired theoretical comparison supplies the initial constraints, and the resulting word properties determine whether additional matching is needed. This keeps the manipulation tied to measurable characteristics of the items.
pages.visual: The two query links distinguish “Generate Lists of Items with Specific Lexical Characteristics” from “Submit lists of Items to retrieve Lexical Characteristics.” They represent different starting points for the same task of making stimulus properties explicit.

pages.title: Selecting lexical fields and constraints
pages.c: A database query separates the fields to retrieve from the constraints used to select items. Length and frequency can both be included as output fields, while minimum and maximum values restrict which words enter the list. Retrieving both variables makes it possible to examine whether one changes systematically with the other.
support: For a frequency comparison, the goal is to obtain items that differ on frequency while controlling a plausible confound such as length. A query with frequency constraints can identify candidates, and their returned lengths help determine whether further selection is required. The database does not decide the experimental comparison on its own.
pages.d: The researcher translates a design goal into measurable selection criteria. A frequency field defines the scale being used, and numeric bounds define the acceptable range. The choice of additional output fields determines which possible confounds can be checked in the resulting items.
pages.visual: The interface has checkboxes for Length and frequency measures, plus minimum and maximum boxes for the selected frequency field. The displayed form makes the distinction between requesting a variable and constraining its values concrete.

pages.title: Frequency distributions and word length
pages.c: English **word frequency is highly uneven**. When the 200 most frequent words are divided into ten ordered groups of twenty, the mean frequency falls sharply from the first group to the next. A small number of words account for a large amount of usage. The length pattern moves in the opposite direction, with the highest-frequency groups containing shorter words on average.
support: The steep frequency drop illustrates Zipf’s law in the ranked vocabulary. The length relationship creates the practical confound for a naming study. Selecting very frequent words naturally selects many short words, so a random low-frequency comparison will usually differ in more than frequency.
pages.d: The two graphs answer different questions about the same ordered groups. One describes how often their words occur. The other describes how many letters their words contain. Their opposing trends explain why independently meaningful word properties can be difficult to manipulate separately.
pages.visual: Both horizontal axes index the ten frequency-ranked groups. Mean frequency per million is on the upper vertical axis, and mean length in letters is on the lower one. Frequency drops rapidly while average length generally rises across the groups.

pages.title: Comparing high- and low-frequency length distributions
pages.c: The **length distributions** of high- and low-frequency words differ substantially. In the comparison of 467 high-frequency words with 467 randomly selected low-frequency words, the high-frequency distribution is centered at a shorter length. Fewer than a quarter of the high-frequency words are as long as the median low-frequency word.
support: A boxplot summarizes a distribution rather than only its average. The median marks the middle of the observations, while the box spans the middle half. Comparing both boxes shows that the relationship is broad across the samples, rather than a result produced by one unusually short or long word.
pages.d: This comparison explains why random sampling is not sufficient for matching. Randomly choosing low-frequency words reflects the natural relation between frequency and length. It does not make that relation disappear from the experimental materials.
pages.visual: HF and LF label the two word-frequency groups. The vertical axis represents word length, and the LF box and median sit above their HF counterparts. The limited overlap around the medians makes the potential length confound easy to see.

pages.title: Matching on a confounding variable
pages.c: To separate frequency from length, the low-frequency comparison should be **selected deliberately rather than at random**. Researchers can choose relatively long high-frequency words and relatively short low-frequency words so that the two conditions have comparable lengths while retaining their frequency difference.
support: Matching changes the relationship between conditions in the experimental sample. It does not claim that frequency and length are unrelated in the language. The purpose is to compare naming performance under a design where length is held similar, allowing the frequency difference to be evaluated more directly.
pages.d: The matching problem is solved by selecting from the overlapping parts of the distributions. Suitable words are less typical of their frequency groups, but they make the desired contrast possible. The important check is whether the final groups actually differ on frequency while agreeing on length.
pages.visual: The same HF and LF boxplots reveal where overlap can be found. Choosing toward the longer end of HF and the shorter end of LF moves the two experimental samples toward a common length range.

pages.title: Frequency effects after length matching
pages.c: Oldfield and Wingfield **matched high- and low-frequency words for length** and still found a robust frequency effect. This result distinguishes an effect associated with frequency from an explanation based entirely on the typical length difference between frequent and infrequent words.
support: The logic depends on the controlled comparison. If length were the whole explanation, making length comparable should remove the naming difference attributed to frequency. Its persistence supports a contribution beyond length. The design turns a correlation among word properties into a more informative comparison between conditions.
pages.d: A confound is addressed by changing the materials or procedure so that its prediction differs from the prediction of the proposed explanation. Here, frequency remains different and length becomes similar. That separation is what gives the persistent frequency effect its evidential value.
pages.visual: The critical comparison is between length-matched frequency groups. The result is a surviving naming difference, rather than the original observation that common words happen to be shorter.

pages.title: Matching several properties of a word set
pages.c: Careful word selection often involves **several dimensions at once**. Cortese and Simpson’s materials illustrate matching regular and irregular words across multiple lexical characteristics. Their table includes properties such as frequency, familiarity, imageability, length and phonological or orthographic measures. Good stimulus design checks the characteristics relevant to the intended comparison.
support: Matching also changes the sample of words being studied. Because correlations such as the frequency–length relationship are real features of the language, selecting around them can produce an unusual combination of items. Imposing many constraints can leave very small groups, as in the ten words per cell described for this study.
pages.d: The design problem is a tradeoff between isolating a variable and retaining an interpretable stimulus set. A very close match on many measurements is useful, but the resulting items still have to be examined as words drawn from a language. The sample size and the basis of the measurements remain part of that evaluation.
pages.visual: The table organizes item means into regular and irregular groups with additional subcolumns. Each row represents another property that could differ unintentionally. Reading across a row checks the comparison between conditions, while reading down a column describes the selected items.

pages.title: Task demands and participants’ awareness
pages.c: Many psycholinguistic effects arise from processes that participants are not consciously monitoring. A person naming drawings ordinarily does not deliberately compute the frequency or length of each name. This makes it possible to measure effects of lexical properties through a simple task without asking participants to describe the underlying process.
support: Other measurements, such as norming ratings, deliberately ask participants for judgments about words. Fillers can be included among the critical items to shape the task context. The relevant design question is what the participant is being asked to do and whether that behavior provides the intended evidence.
pages.d: A task instruction and the mechanism of interest are not always the same thing. Naming a picture is the instructed behavior, while the effect of a word’s properties on naming latency is the evidence used to study production. Keeping these levels separate helps explain why a simple overt task can reveal an implicit process.
pages.visual: The cartoon illustrates a participant thinking about what response an experimenter wants. The text contrasts that concern with processes such as ordinary picture naming, where lexical properties can affect behavior without being the participant’s deliberate focus.

pages.title: Choosing a dependent measure
pages.c: Eye movements, brain responses, reaction time and accuracy can reveal distinctions that participants are not directly controlling. EEG and fMRI measure aspects of brain activity, while eye tracking measures where and when people look. These measures can serve as **dependent variables** for testing how different kinds of stimuli are processed.
support: A difference in brain response can be informative even when no overt response is required. If two stimulus classes produce different patterns, that provides evidence that the participant’s processing distinguishes them. The experimental value of the measure can therefore concern the information being processed as well as the location of activity in the brain.
pages.d: The choice of measure determines which aspect of processing becomes observable. Response time captures timing, accuracy captures success, and gaze can reveal the coordination of looking with another task. A useful design connects the measured behavior to the process named in its hypothesis.
pages.visual: The labeled examples distinguish eye tracking, EEG and fMRI from a tachistoscope used to control brief stimulus presentation. Measuring a response and controlling presentation are different experimental functions.

pages.title: Belke, Meyer and Damian’s semantic-blocking study
pages.c: Belke, Meyer and Damian’s 2005 study used **cyclic semantic blocking** to examine picture naming. Participants repeatedly named sets of objects whose names were either semantically related or unrelated. Naming was slower in related sets once the objects had already been encountered. The experiments used changes in presentation, eye tracking and new items to investigate where this cost arises.
support: Experiment 1 established that the blocking effect appeared after the objects had been named once. Experiment 2 presented objects simultaneously and found blocking in naming latency and gaze duration, but not a significant blocking effect in the gaze-to-speech lag. Experiment 3 showed that the cost generalized to new names from the same categories.
pages.d: The three experiments connect a behavioral effect to a proposed processing locus. The important evidence is the pattern across conditions and measures. Related context increases a cost of selecting names even though repetition produces its own facilitation.
pages.visual: The paper title identifies the task as picture naming and the manipulation as semantic blocking. Its abstract defines homogeneous sets as semantically related and heterogeneous sets as unrelated, and distinguishes gaze duration from the lag between gaze offset and articulation onset.

pages.title: Mapping a word-production model onto production stages
pages.c: The WEAVER++ model organizes information about producing a word into **conceptual, syntactic and word-form levels**. It is especially concerned with activation and selection for individual words. A general sentence-production model separates a message level, a functional level, a positional level, phonological encoding and articulation. The two models therefore organize related processes at different scales.
support: The syntactic information in a single-word model can concern features such as number and gender. This is not identical to building a whole sentence’s positional frame. Comparing the models requires attention to what each representation is supposed to encode rather than matching boxes by name alone.
pages.d: The conceptual and lemma portions of WEAVER++ are central to the semantic-blocking explanation. They allow activation of a concept to influence candidate word representations. The comparison with the larger production model helps locate this competition before the final sequence of sounds and articulatory actions.
pages.visual: The highlighted regions emphasize conceptual and syntactic or functional information above word-form encoding. The lower word-form network represents additional processing that is distinct from selecting a lemma. The correspondence is approximate because one model focuses on words and the other on utterances.

pages.title: Spreading activation can create competition
pages.c: Related concepts share connections in a **spreading-activation model**. Activating duck can also activate properties and categories connected with other animals, such as fish, snake and mouse. It may seem that making these names more active should always make them easier to produce, but a naming task also requires selecting one candidate over the others.
support: A semantically homogeneous set activates multiple related candidates. That activity can help make the target available while also making its competitors available. The effect on naming time depends on the selection process, not simply on whether the target receives some additional activation.
pages.d: The distinction between availability and selection is essential. A representation can become active without being the one chosen for speech. When several candidates receive support from shared semantic information, deciding which lemma to select can take longer.
pages.visual: The upper network contains concepts and features such as animal, bird, swim and scales. Duck, fish, snake and mouse connect with overlapping portions of that network. The lower lemma nodes represent word candidates that receive activation from their corresponding concepts.

pages.title: Activation and lemma selection are different processes
pages.c: WEAVER++ distinguishes **activation of candidate lemmas from selection** of the lemma to be spoken. Selection time depends on the target’s activation relative to the total activation across lemmas. Increasing activation of several semantically related competitors can therefore slow selection even when the target itself is active.
support: Activating duck can spread activation to related animal concepts and their lemmas. Category feedback adds collateral activation to other members of the category. If several candidates remain active, the target is less dominant relative to the whole set. The speaker then takes longer to select the correct name.
pages.d: The predicted cost follows from relative activation. A target considered alone might appear easier to retrieve after semantic activation, but the model evaluates it in relation to competitors. This explains how semantic relatedness can produce interference in naming rather than only facilitation.
pages.visual: The concept network fans out through shared properties and categories, then reaches the corresponding lemma nodes. Those connections illustrate why selecting duck can be affected by activation of fish, snake and mouse even though only one name is required.

pages.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous naming contexts
pages.c: Participants named pictures across eight presentation cycles. **Homogeneous**, or HOM, contexts contained semantically related objects such as duck, mouse, fish and snake. Heterogeneous, or HET, contexts combined unrelated names such as duck, saw, chair and bus. A target such as duck could therefore be compared across related and unrelated contexts.
support: Repeating the same identities across cycles allows two kinds of comparison. Response times can change with repeated exposure, and they can differ between semantic contexts. The graph tracks both by plotting response time separately for HOM and HET across the presentation cycles.
pages.d: The central contrast is the semantic relationship among the items surrounding a target. The picture and its name are not intrinsically a HOM or HET item. They belong to a condition because of the other objects in their naming set.
pages.visual: The horizontal axis shows cycles one through eight, and the vertical axis shows response time in milliseconds. Separate HOM and HET lines track related and unrelated contexts. Their shared early drop and later separation represent different effects that must be interpreted separately.

pages.title: Repetition facilitation and semantic blocking
pages.c: **Two effects** appear in the naming-time pattern. Repetition makes naming faster, producing a large drop after the initial cycle. Semantic blocking makes naming relatively slower in homogeneous than heterogeneous contexts once the objects have been named. The same experiment therefore contains facilitation from repeated identities and interference from semantic context.
support: The two effects are not contradictory. Repetition is a comparison across encounters with an item. Blocking is a comparison between related and unrelated contexts at a given stage of the experiment. A condition can become faster over time while remaining slower than the comparison condition.
pages.d: Follow the direction of each comparison. Moving along one line across cycles reveals repetition-related improvement. Comparing HOM and HET within a cycle reveals the semantic-context cost. Confusing these comparisons would turn two separable effects into one misleading overall description.
pages.visual: Both curves descend sharply from the first cycle. In later cycles, HOM responses are generally slower than HET responses. The vertical gap between the curves represents blocking, while the drop along the curves represents repetition facilitation.

pages.title: Testing visual similarity as a competing explanation
pages.c: Semantically related objects might also look alike, so **visual recognition** is a possible alternative explanation for slower naming in homogeneous sets. Belke and colleagues addressed this by norming the stimuli so that within-category objects were not more visually similar on average than objects from different categories.
support: They also conducted a control experiment that blocked visual similarity. That manipulation produced a different time course, with an effect in the first block of trials. The semantic-blocking effect in the main experiment emerged after the initial naming cycle. Matching and the contrasting control pattern jointly distinguish the semantic result from a simple visual-similarity account.
pages.d: A strong control gives the alternative mechanism its own test. The visual-similarity account predicts a relationship to how much the pictures resemble each other. Matching that property and observing a different pattern when it is manipulated directly makes it harder to attribute the semantic effect to the same source.
pages.visual: The two numbered controls have different roles. Norming checks the selected pictures, while the control experiment tests what visual similarity itself does to naming. The difference in when the effect appears is crucial to the comparison.

pages.title: Simultaneous displays with serial naming
pages.c: Belke and colleagues tested whether the semantic-blocking result depended on seeing objects one at a time. A related study by Hermens and colleagues had presented several objects simultaneously without finding the same effect. The new task therefore placed **four pictures in a display together** while requiring their names to be produced one after another.
support: This separates simultaneous visual availability from serial speech output. The participant can see the set as a whole, but still has to select and articulate each object name in sequence. Measuring the resulting behavior tests a property of the task rather than treating a difference between studies as a theoretical explanation by itself.
pages.d: The manipulation changes how the objects are presented while preserving the need to name individual targets. This makes it possible to ask whether semantic competition persists when the next objects are already visible.
pages.visual: The illustrated display contains duck, snake, fish and mouse at the same time. Their shared animal category makes a homogeneous display, while the instruction to produce their names serially defines the response sequence.

pages.title: Coordinating gaze with successive object names
pages.c: **Eye tracking** adds a time-resolved measure to the multiple-object naming task. The participant looks at one object, shifts gaze to another and produces the object names in sequence. The eyes can move on before articulation of the previous name begins, so looking and speaking are coordinated without being perfectly simultaneous.
support: The timing diagram separates the interval spent looking at each object from the onset of its spoken name. This permits a naming delay to be divided into components rather than treated as a single undifferentiated response time. Different components can then be compared across homogeneous and heterogeneous displays.
pages.d: The point of recording eye movements is to identify where in the sequence the semantic-context difference appears. If relatedness changes how long the eyes remain on an object, it affects a different measured interval than a change occurring only after the eyes leave it.
pages.visual: GD marks gaze duration on each object, and Art marks the onset of articulating its name. The descending arrangement shows a shift from one object to the next while speech follows behind. The labeled lag lies between the end of looking and the beginning of the corresponding name.

pages.title: Gaze duration and eye-to-speech lag
pages.c: **Gaze duration** is the time spent looking at an object during the naming sequence. Evidence links the timing of gaze shifts to lemma selection. The eye-to-speech lag is the interval after gaze leaves that object and before its name begins. Phonological encoding and gesture planning can continue during this interval without continued visual support.
support: These two measures help distinguish stages that are combined in an overall naming latency. A semantic effect on gaze duration is consistent with a cost in the selection process coordinated with looking. An effect on lag would instead concern processing that continues after the gaze shift.
pages.d: The labels describe observable intervals, while the stage assignments are theoretical interpretations supported by the task. The experiment becomes informative by asking whether the semantic manipulation affects the two intervals in the same way or selectively affects one.
pages.visual: Each GD box ends where gaze moves to the next object. The following Lag box extends to Art for the previous object. The staggered boxes show that an object’s sound and movement plan can still be completed after visual attention has shifted.

pages.title: An eye–mouth coordination demonstration
pages.c: An eye–mouth coordination demonstration follows looking while a speaker describes an event. The supplied example concerns correctly naming the patient in “The horse is kicking a cow.” The horse is the agent performing the action, and the cow is the patient affected by it. Producing the sentence requires selecting those referents and coordinating their names with the event description.
support: The methodological connection is between the event being described, the locations inspected and the words produced. Those measurements can reveal when information about a participant becomes relevant to sentence formulation. The example complements the object-naming task by making the relation between looking and a meaningful utterance explicit.
pages.d: Agent and patient identify roles in the event rather than positions on the screen. The eye record becomes interpretable when it is aligned with the speaker’s choices and spoken words. That alignment is what makes eye–mouth coordination useful for studying production.
pages.visual: The static preview labels the example “Accurately labeling a patient” and gives the target sentence. Its text establishes the event roles. The linked demonstration is separate from the supplied static page.

pages.title: The semantic cost appears in gaze duration
pages.c: The eye-tracking experiment separates overall speech duration, gaze duration and eye-to-speech lag. Speech duration decreases with practice but does not show a semantic-blocking effect. **Gaze duration does show blocking** after the first cycle, with longer looking in homogeneous contexts. The lag measure has no significant blocking effect.
support: The repetition-related changes and the semantic-context contrast must again be kept separate. A measure can become shorter over cycles without differing reliably between HOM and HET. In the lag graph, the small numerical difference even goes in the opposite direction, but it is not statistically significant.
pages.d: The important evidence is selective sensitivity. The semantic manipulation changes the interval spent looking at the object more clearly than the measured intervals associated with speaking duration or processing after gaze offset. That pattern helps constrain where the naming cost arises.
pages.visual: The three panels share presentation cycle on the horizontal axis. The upper panel tracks speech duration, the middle panel gaze duration, and the lower panel gaze-to-speech lag. The reliable HOM–HET difference in the middle panel is the key dissociation.

pages.title: Relating the timing pattern to production stages
pages.c: The selective gaze-duration effect supports a **lemma-selection account** of semantic blocking. Looking is coordinated with selecting the object’s name, so a longer gaze interval in homogeneous sets fits increased competition among related lemmas. The absence of a significant lag effect provides no parallel evidence for a blocking cost in the measured interval after gaze leaves the object.
support: The stage interpretation connects speech duration with the gesture level, gaze duration with lemma selection, and lag with downstream phonological encoding. The repetition-related reductions across the task do not establish a semantic-blocking effect at each of those levels. The relevant comparison is whether HOM and HET differ within each measure.
pages.d: The conclusion is based on the combination of a positive gaze effect and the pattern in the other measures. The data identify where the manipulation produces its clearest measured cost. They do not turn a nonsignificant contrast into a claim that the corresponding processing stage is absent.
pages.visual: The arrows explicitly connect the top, middle and bottom panels with gesture, lemma-selection and phonological-encoding interpretations. The middle graph’s separation after the first cycle is the evidence that carries the selection argument.

pages.title: Blocking transfers to new category members
pages.c: Experiment 3 tested whether semantic blocking depended on repeatedly naming the same individual objects. New items from the same categories were introduced in cycle five. Naming became much slower when those new items appeared, but the homogeneous-context cost remained. The effect therefore **generalized beyond the particular names** that had been practiced.
support: The spike in response time reflects the loss of the accumulated repetition advantage for the old items. The continued HOM–HET difference shows that semantic blocking survives that change in item identity. Comparing cycle five with the initial cycle helps separate prior category experience from simply having named a particular object before.
pages.d: The experiment changes the identities while preserving the relevant category relation. If the effect were only a special consequence of repeating a particular list of names, transferring it to previously unnamed category members would be unexpected. The surviving cost supports a process linked to the semantic context.
pages.visual: The arrow marks new items at cycle five, where both response-time curves rise sharply. Despite that shared rise, HOM remains slower than HET. The repeated-category comparison is therefore still visible after the identity-based practice advantage is disrupted.

pages.title: Locating semantic blocking through converging controls
pages.c: The semantic-blocking explanation is constrained by **several comparisons**. Visual recognition is tested through picture matching and a visual-similarity control. A phonological explanation is weakened when the names are not phonologically similar and the cost appears in gaze duration rather than significantly in the eye-to-speech lag. Generalization to new items separates blocking from a purely item-specific repetition effect.
support: These controls address different points in the path from recognizing an object to producing its name. Their value comes from narrowing the explanation together. The remaining account centers on the selection of a lemma among semantically activated competitors.
pages.d: An experiment is more informative when competing explanations are translated into distinct predictions. Similar-looking pictures, similar-sounding words and repeated identities are three different candidate sources of interference. The research program uses different comparisons to evaluate each one.
pages.visual: The listed alternatives correspond to recognizing the picture, planning the word’s sound form and repeating a specific item. Treating them as separate hypotheses explains why more than one control is required.

pages.title: What each control contributes to the inference
pages.c: The **visual-recognition alternative** is addressed by norming and matching the pictures and by a separate visual-similarity control. The phonological alternative is examined through the lack of shared sound form and the distinction between gaze duration and eye-to-speech lag. The repeated-list alternative is tested by introducing new items from the same categories.
support: The generalization result is especially important because it changes the actual names while preserving category history. The eye-tracking result is important for a different reason, because it divides the naming sequence into measured intervals. These designs contribute complementary evidence for locating the effect around lemma selection.
pages.d: The question mark attached to phonological encoding reflects that the timing measures support an interpretation rather than directly observing a hidden processing stage. Gaze duration changes with semantic context, while the lag contrast is not significant. That pattern supplies the evidence for comparing the accounts.
pages.visual: Each major alternative is paired with its test. Visual recognition has matching and a control experiment. Phonological encoding has sound-form and timing comparisons. Specific list repetition has transfer to new items. This mapping is the logic of the experimental argument.

pages.title: Turning an alternative explanation into an experiment
pages.c: A useful experimental question begins by specifying **another process** that could explain an observed effect. Word frequency is correlated with length, age of acquisition, imageability and contextual diversity. An apparent frequency effect might therefore be partly associated with one of those properties. Naming a picture also includes object recognition and response selection, which can be examined separately.
support: The next step is to design a comparison that distinguishes the explanations. Matching a suspected confound, manipulating it directly, changing item identity or adding a different dependent measure can reveal whether the same effect follows the alternative variable. Belke and colleagues’ controls illustrate these different forms of comparison.
pages.d: The phrase “couldn’t it just be” becomes scientifically useful when the proposed alternative is specific enough to predict a result. Naming a candidate variable is the beginning. The design must show what would differ if that variable accounted for the effect.
pages.visual: The two lists distinguish properties of stimuli from processes within the task. Length and imageability characterize the words, while recognition and response selection characterize operations performed during naming. Both can generate competing explanations.

pages.title: Assigned reading · Diehl, Lotto and Holt

questions.stem: Why is word length a confound in an unmatched comparison of naming times for frequent and infrequent words?
choices: Frequency groups also tend to differ in length, so length supplies another explanation for the timing difference.
Word length is the dependent variable in every picture-naming experiment.
All high-frequency and low-frequency words have the same length.
A confound is any measurement that participants can consciously report.
questions.why: Frequent words tend to be shorter, so the manipulation can change both properties together.

questions.stem: What does a frequency effect that survives matching on length support?
choices: The naming difference is not entirely explained by the groups’ original length difference.
Frequency and length are unrelated throughout the language.
The study has removed every possible lexical confound.
Long words must always be named faster than short words.
questions.why: The matched comparison keeps frequency different while making length comparable, testing the length-only explanation.

questions.stem: What tradeoff can arise from matching word lists on many dimensions?
choices: The remaining items may be atypical combinations or leave very small samples.
Matching automatically increases the number of available stimuli.
Matching makes the chosen items a random sample of all words.
Matching prevents a researcher from measuring naming latency.
questions.why: The source explicitly notes artificial stimulus environments and small cells as consequences of very fine-grained matching.

questions.stem: Why can spreading activation slow picture naming in WEAVER++?
choices: Related competitors become active, reducing the target’s dominance during lemma selection.
Activation always removes every competing lemma from the lexicon.
The target is selected before conceptual information becomes active.
Related concepts necessarily have identical pronunciations.
questions.why: Selection depends on relative activation, so collateral activation can increase competition even when the target receives activation.

questions.stem: Which comparison isolates semantic context for a target such as duck?
choices: Naming duck among related animal names versus among unrelated names.
Naming a familiar duck picture versus viewing an empty screen.
Comparing the spelling of duck with the spelling of the same word.
Comparing two conditions that contain exactly the same category relationships.
questions.why: HOM and HET differ in the semantic relationship among the names within the set.

questions.stem: How can repetition facilitation and semantic blocking occur in the same experiment?
choices: Naming becomes faster with repetition while remaining slower in homogeneous than heterogeneous contexts.
Blocking means response times must increase on every successive cycle.
Repetition facilitation is defined as slower naming of semantically related items.
The two effects concern the same comparison and therefore cannot coexist.
questions.why: The across-cycle improvement and the within-cycle HOM–HET contrast are different comparisons.

questions.stem: How did the visual-similarity control help evaluate the semantic-blocking effect?
choices: It produced a different time course, with an effect already in the first block.
It eliminated all semantic relationships from the main experiment’s names.
It showed that every animal picture was visually identical.
It measured only the length of written words.
questions.why: The distinct time course, together with picture norming, argues against treating the main effect as a simple visual-similarity effect.

questions.stem: What is the eye-to-speech lag in the multiple-object naming task?
choices: The interval from looking away from an object to beginning its spoken name.
The entire duration of articulating all four names.
The time from picture onset until the participant first sees any object.
The amount of time spent looking at a single object.
questions.why: Gaze duration ends at gaze offset. The lag follows that offset and ends at the name’s articulatory onset.

questions.stem: Which timing pattern supports the lemma-selection interpretation of semantic blocking?
choices: Blocking appears in gaze duration after the first cycle, without a significant blocking effect in eye-to-speech lag.
Only overall speech duration shows a reliable semantic-blocking effect.
All three timing measures increase equally in homogeneous contexts.
Gaze duration shows no relationship to the semantic manipulation.
questions.why: The selective gaze effect fits a cost in the process coordinated with gaze shifts, while the lag measure provides no parallel significant contrast.

questions.stem: Why are new items introduced in cycle five informative?
choices: They remove the old items’ repetition advantage while testing whether blocking transfers within the category.
They make homogeneous and heterogeneous sets identical in semantic composition.

written.prompt: Explain how length matching helps interpret a word-frequency effect in picture naming.
answer: High-frequency names tend to be shorter, so an unmatched latency difference could be associated with either property.
Select high- and low-frequency names with comparable lengths. A surviving frequency effect supports an explanation beyond the original length difference.

written.prompt: Explain how Belke and colleagues used different controls to locate the semantic-blocking effect.
answer: Norming and a visual-similarity experiment address picture recognition. The visual control has a different time course from semantic blocking.
Gaze duration shows blocking after the first cycle, while eye-to-speech lag has no significant blocking effect. This timing pattern supports a lemma-selection interpretation.
The effect transfers to new items from the same categories, showing that it is not only a consequence of repeating particular names.
